Google STEP Internship Process 
(Offcampus) 
 
Sneha Singh 
B-Tech Information Technology 
VJTI Mumbai 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
SECTIONS - 
1.​ The process 
2.​ Approaching a Google Interview 
3.​ Suggestions 
4.​ Resources

What is the Google STEP Internship? 
The Google STEP Internship (Student Training in Engineering Program) 
now called ASD Internship (Associate Software Developer Intern) is a 
12-week paid summer internship at Google, designed for first- and 
second-year undergraduates in computer science or related fields. Interns 
collaborate in small teams with full-time Googlers, working on real 
software projects while receiving mentorship and professional 
development. 
 
 
SECTION 1 : The process 
(FYI: Each round is eliminatory which implies, you can advance to round 
(x+1) only if you clear round x) 
 
 
Round 1 : Initial Application 
You can apply for the STEP through https://careers.google.com/. The 
application process contains filling your personal details and resume. The 
initial shortlisting is purely on the basis of resume, so have a professional 
resume. Attaching the template I used for my resume. Try to have at least 
2–3 projects, good coding profiles and decent CGPA. Mention relevant 
achievements, experiences and certifications. 
 
Round 2 : Telephonic Round 
In this round I was asked everything about my technical background like 
my projects, CGPA, coding profiles, contests performance, proficiency in 
coding, number of questions solved till date, etc.

Round 3 : Interview 1 (4th November 2024) 
Duration : 45 minutes 
 
The interview started by both of us introducing yourselves. Then the 
interviewer quickly shared an online editor link with me and pasted the 
question on it. The question was of LeetCode Hard difficulty.I was able to 
solve it within the given time. It concluded with me asking him some 
questions. The interviewer seemed satisfied with my overall performance. 
 
Round 4 : Interview 2 (11th November 2024) 
Duration : 45 minutes 
 
The interview began with quick introductions, and then we moved straight 
to the question. The question was of Leetcode medium difficulty. I was able 
to solve it in around 15–20 minutes. The interviewer then asked three 
follow-up questions in succession, each presented only after I had solved 
the previous one. The follow-ups increased in difficulty. In the end, the 
interviewer seemed satisfied with my performance. 
 
Verdict :  
 
 
After refreshing my inbox every single day😂, and waiting for around two 
weeks, I was finally informed that I was SELECTEDDD🎉🥳. I was

extremely happy to see all the years of hard work and sleepless nights 
finally bear fruit. 
Note: The verdict process may take anywhere from one day to one month, 
depending on the evaluation cycle and internal timelines. 
 
 
SECTION 2 : How to approach a Google 
Interview? (Important) 
●​ Self Introduction: Since you have only 45 minutes in total, having 
a short & sweet intro would save time 
 
●​ Lead the communication: DON’T be a silent coder. Be ALOUD 
throughout the interview and lead the communication. Leading the 
communication is as important as solving the problem. Candidates 
who do both are the ones who stand out. Even when you are coding 
the problem, keep narrating what you are writing. This keeps both of 
you on track and keeps the interview lively. 
 
●​ Summarise the problem: Start by briefly summarising your 
understanding of the problem. This shows the interviewer that you’ve 
grasped the correct problem and creates a positive impression 
 
●​ Ask clarifying questions: Google’s interview questions are 
intentionally open-ended — they don’t always provide all the details 
upfront. It’s important to ask clarifying questions to understand the 
requirements fully. I’ve listed some examples of such clarifying 
questions in this article: Clarifying Questions List. 
 
●​ After this, start discussing your approach with the interviewer. 
Do NOT directly jump into silent coding. Usually start with the brute 
force approach and build it towards the optimal one.

●​ Discuss the time and space complexities of the approach in 
detail. 
 
●​ Dry Run: Once both of you agree over the approach, do a quick dry 
run on the editor over a few test-cases. This shows your capability to 
find errors in any code without needing to run it. 
 
●​ Write neat, modular code: Writing neat code helps ensure that 
future requirements can be addressed without heavily modifying 
existing code. Break your solution into clear, well-defined functions. 
For example, in my second interview, I was able to work quickly 
despite multiple follow-up questions because my code was neat and 
modular, making it easy to adapt to any requisite changes and 
optimisations. 
 
●​ Good Naming: Write clean and readable code. Give meaningful 
variable naming and use camelCase throughout the code. Readability 
is just as important as correctness, especially in Google interviews. 
 
●​ Listen to the interviewer: Consistently listen to what the 
interviewer is saying. He/She might drop some hints where you are 
stuck. 
 
●​ Be quick but not hurried: The interviewer may expect you to solve 
follow up questions. So try to solve the initial question given to you as 
early as possible. 
 
●​ Edge cases: Always practice thinking of your own edge cases instead 
of relying on platforms like LeetCode to point them out. In interviews, 
the interviewer won’t help you identify edge cases, it’s your 
responsibility.

SECTION 3 : Suggestions 
●​ Don’t expect easy questions — Even though STEP is a second-year 
opportunity, the interviews often involve challenging DSA problems 
that test both your depth and breadth of knowledge. Try to cover 
every topic of DSA and do not skip hard questions. 
 
●​ Apply early — STEP receives a huge amount of applications every year 
so submitting your application early can increase your chances of 
being considered. 
 
●​ Apply through referrals — Reach out to Google employees, interns, or 
apprentices to request referrals and increase the visibility of your 
application. 
 
●​ Participate in Google hackathons — These events not only help you 
build skills but also make your profile visible to recruiters 
beforehand. 
 
●​ Think of multiple approaches when solving problems. Over time, I’ve 
realised that work in most MNCs is less about just getting one 
solution that meets the requirements and more about evaluating, 
discussing, and comparing different possible approaches. 
 
●​ Practice doing dry runs on editors as well. 
 
●​ Always analyse time and space complexities of problems you solve. 
 
●​ Practice explaining your approaches in a clear and precise manner 
with your friends and peers, as good communication and explanation 
skills are equally essential. 
 
●​ Take up mock interviews.

ourse-sheet-2

ailed-video-solutions
